science-mind-857fe5e3ca.headline: Two AI companies reveal ‘Earth-shattering’ solutions to major maths problem
science-mind-857fe5e3ca.fulltext:
Two AI companies have released “Earth-shattering” solutions to a problem related to P versus NP, considered one of the most difficult puzzles in mathematics. Coming a few days after a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the achievement is a further sign that the pace of progress being made by AI in maths is unlike anything ever seen before.
P versus NP relates to how difficult some problems are to solve using a computer. P problems are relatively simple to solve, but NP problems quickly become drastically more difficult as their size increases. If P could be proved to be the same as NP, then we would have a radically faster way to solve a host of computationally intensive problems, and there would be a dramatic effect on society: computer encryption would break, logistical and engineering problems could be highly optimised, and new drugs could be discovered more easily.
It is one of the seven Millennium Prize problems published by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, which promise a $1 million award to anyone who can solve them. One of those, the Poincaré conjecture, fell in 2010. Two others have fallen to AI: the Navier-Stokes puzzle in September and the Riemann hypothesis last week.
Advertisement
The new AI results concern VP versus VNP, a problem posed after mathematicians and computer scientists realised the importance of P versus NP, but made little progress towards a solution. The idea was to replace the binary logic of computers with arithmetic, which imposes a more structured problem set. It is supposed to be a stepping stone along the way to P vs NP – not necessarily something that would lead directly to a solution, but something that would widen our understanding and help clear a path to more on P vs NP.
Yesterday, Anthropic quietly published its VP versus VNP finding on its GitHub page with no wider announcement. The work proves that VNP isn’t contained within VP and that some classes of problems are simply difficult to solve no matter what. The company said the discovery was made by an internal research version of its Claude model, which also wrote the paper and a formalisation, a conversion of the proof to computer code that allows it to be methodically and logically picked apart and proved correct. “No human mathematician has checked the proof,” the company said.
On the same day, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI released a paper on GitHub setting out its own solution to the same problem, also including a formalisation. The two solutions are similar in some ways but diverge on key points. Neither company responded to a request for comment, but the timestamps of the uploads suggest Anthropic beat OpenAI to the prize by about 6 hours.
Tom Gur at the University of Cambridge was surprised by the news and says he thought many other discoveries would be made before VP versus VNP was solved.
“If you’d have asked me in what now feels like ancient history, which would be, I don’t know, August, I would have told you that I don’t think I will live to see it,” says Gur. “We are seeing here decades of progress in days. It’s an exciting time to be alive.”
Mathematicians argue about the relative difficulty of the two problems, and how far a solution to VP versus VNP gets us to a solution to P versus NP. “But one thing you can say for sure is that this is Earth-shattering progress,” says Gur. “It’s just so far beyond the range of techniques that we had before.”
The difficulty facing mathematicians working on either puzzle – VP versus VNP or P versus NP – is that proving that a problem previously thought to be very hard is actually easy is straightforward: simply show an algorithm that solves it easily. But proving that a problem or set of problems is actually very hard, and will always remain so, requires evidence that there is no algorithm that can be written which can solve it easily.
“The reality is that we have a very, very, very limited arsenal of tools to prove this limitation [that some algorithms are intrinsically hard],” says Gur. The proof of VP versus VNP is an extremely powerful tool, but the question is how generalisable it is, he says. “I think we need, as a community, more time to study these results to understand.”
Varun Kanade at the University of Oxford thinks the new proofs will help with – but not directly lead to – a solution for P versus NP. “It does get us closer in the sense that it makes progress on a problem related to the main one, but my sense is that we will require new techniques for the P v NP question,” he says. “At this point, I have to say that I’m not surprised that AI has made progress on this question, having seen the recent announcement of the proof of the Riemann hypothesis.”
But Ben Livshits at Imperial College London says not everyone will be buoyed by the discoveries and the way they were achieved.
“AI is now doing research-level mathematics and theoretical computer science, and I don’t think we’ve properly thought through the longer-term effects,” says Livshits. “For theoretical computer scientists, many of whom have spent years or whole careers on these problems, it’s a very mixed blessing, and several have already said so.”

ai-754f867302.headline: Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups
ai-754f867302.fulltext:
Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.
Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.
The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.
The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.
Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.

world-7f6a68b604.headline: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
world-7f6a68b604.fulltext:
The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
- Published
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.
Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.
Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.
And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.
Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.
"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.
Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.
At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.
Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.
India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

world-0c76e6617a.headline: Chinese cobalt firms race to beat DR Congo’s export ban on key battery material
world-0c76e6617a.fulltext:

CMOC expedites shipments before indefinite suspension, which the world’s top exporting country says targets a ‘persistent imbalance’
The Democratic Republic of Congo, home to the world’s largest cobalt reserves, will suspend exports of the critical battery metal from November 30 until further notice, prompting Chinese operators with assets in the country to accelerate shipments over the coming week.
The country’s Authority for the Regulation and Control of Strategic Mineral Substance Markets (Arecoms) said on Monday that the suspension would apply to all cobalt produced nationally, covering both industrial mines and artisanal output.
“We learned of the announcement [on Tuesday] morning,” said an investor relations employee at Shanghai-based CMOC Group, which is the world’s largest mined cobalt producer and controls two major copper-cobalt mines in Congo. “The company will expedite cargoes in the week ahead, and some are already en route.”
CMOC would continue to monitor developments, the person said, adding that should the export ban prop up cobalt prices, it would “benefit us as an exporter to some extent”.
Congo’s suspension sought to tackle a “persistent imbalance” in the cobalt market – driven by weak demand, rising inventories and excess supply, Arecoms said in a statement, according to a Monday report by Reuters.
Cobalt is primarily used to make batteries for electric vehicles and mobile phones. The restriction carries direct implications for China, a powerhouse in the battery sector that has scant domestic cobalt resources. The US Geological Survey data puts Congo’s cobalt reserves at 6 million tonnes, 37.5 times China’s.
Chinese firms are no strangers to such export curbs, as this marks the second time Congo has suspended cobalt shipments since February 2025. The previous restriction was also rolled out when cobalt prices came under pressure.
Platts, an independent physical-commodity price provider, assessed European 99.8 per cent cobalt metal at US$18.15 per pound on Friday. The benchmark was 24 per cent lower than at the start of 2026, according to a Monday report by S&P Global.
“The slide in prices stems largely from soft consumer-electronics sales,” said Xiao Wenhao, an analyst at research firm Shanghai Metals Market. “Lithium cobalt oxide cells used in consumer electronics have the highest cobalt loading per kilowatt-hour.”
Xiao said consumer-electronics sales have stayed weak largely because rising memory chip prices have lifted smartphone prices, crimping demand.
Arecoms said it would review the temporary export halt after four months, taking into account cobalt market trends, inventory levels and the global supply-demand balance, according to S&P Global. The previous export suspension ran for more than seven months, during which time cobalt prices increased.
Xiao said this round would also push the metal’s value higher even though demand was set to stay weak. The restriction was “beyond the market’s prior expectations”, she said, adding that Arecoms had sent a “clear and loud” signal to the market.
Yet, the move carried trade-offs, according to analysts. The suspension could further spur Chinese firms to develop substitute cobalt supplies, as they did during the 2025 round. And more companies now were recovering cobalt from spent batteries or expanding operations in other nations, they said.
Huayou Cobalt, a global player based in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, said the suspension would be manageable.
“We hold an annual export quota of just over 1,000 tonnes of contained cobalt from the Congo government,” said an investor relations employee. “A large portion of our cobalt feedstock comes from our mines in Indonesia, so the fallout is limited.”
Before joining the SCMP, Emma was a reporter for a state-run organisation for 16 years.

climate-energy-7855a7b6de.headline: COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya
climate-energy-7855a7b6de.fulltext:
COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, failed to agree on a “pact” that – despite making no clear reference to fossil fuels or adaptation finance – had contained strong signals for oceans.
The “Antalya pact” took up much of the two weeks of negotiating time in Turkey, only to be rejected during the closing plenary by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable countries.
Several countries expressed their regret during the plenary that significant work on advancing ocean-climate action would be lost.
The COP ran nearly 50 hours over time, but did not end with substantive outcomes on several key topics.
For the second year in a row, negotiations on agriculture and food security broke down and will now have to resume next year.
Food-systems advocates were, however, heartened by the explicit inclusion of “agroecology” in a decision within the “just transition work programme”.
Ocean-conservation groups noted an increased focus on ocean-climate links at this year’s COP, but said COP31 did not live up to its promise of being a “blue COP”.
There was also scant new funding for food systems and nature, with just a handful of small pledges to ocean initiatives and two newly announced contributions to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility.
Here, Carbon Brief analyses all of the key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at COP31 – both inside and out of the negotiating rooms.
(See Carbon Brief’s coverage of food, forests, oceans and nature at COP30, COP29, COP28, COP27 and COP26.)
Formal negotiations
Cover decision
The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious – closing plenary in Antalya.
Other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent.
However, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations.
Ultimately, parties did not find consensus on the text, particularly around the removal of any reference to fossil fuels and the lack of concrete climate-finance targets.
The cover text was one of the places in the negotiations where ocean advocates were hoping to see ocean-climate linkages highlighted.
Marine Lecerf, head of international policy at Ocean & Climate Platform, told a press huddle:
“What we’re really asking for right now is to make sure we can recognise ocean-based interlinkages…We’re not asking for a new mandate. We are asking for acceleration of the work that is already undertaken.”
The first draft of the cover decision, published on 16 November, was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion. It was accompanied by a short “presidency note” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text.
This lengthy first draft had 21 references to the ocean, including recognising the impacts of climate change, support for ocean-observing systems, encouraging parties to strengthen ocean-climate action and a multi-year plan for the “ocean and climate change dialogue”, which occurs annually at the Bonn intersessional meetings in June.
Regarding that draft, Steven Guilbeault, former environment minister of Canada, told Carbon Brief:
“I don’t see why the elements that are in the cover decision right now on oceans should be controversial or problematic to any nations. If you’re serious about fighting climate change, there’s nothing in this text regarding oceans that should be problematic for you.”
(Earth Negotiations Bulletin reported that Russia opposed mentions of the ocean in the cover text during the ocean ministerial consultation.)
The next iteration of the text, on 19 November, retained many of the ocean elements, albeit with less detail than the first draft. The second text also removed references to post-2028 ocean work and a proposed high-level ministerial ocean dialogue.
In the end, oceans had 19 mentions in the rejected Antalya pact.
During the final plenary, Fiji’s Dr Sivendra Michael – co-chair of the ocean and climate change dialogue – appealed to the COP31 president to “humbly consolidate” the consensus on ocean as a “standalone ocean decision” and “directly submit” ten paragraphs with no objections in text as a “way to preserve” work done.
Lynda Tabuya, Fiji’s environment and climate change minister, said:
“The ocean-climate nexus is undeniable. We, the people of the Pacific, are deeply indebted, as the ocean is our home, our identity and it is what connects us. There is no climate action without ocean action. We hope this is not lost today and that parties will please consider keeping the ocean text alive.”
Other aspects of the natural world garnered significantly less attention in the cover text.
The final decision failed to mention the Brazil-led roadmap on deforestation, although it was “welcome[d]” in the initial draft. (See: Deforestation.)
Mentions of the “critical role” of forests in carbon storage, food security, biodiversity and community adaptation were also stripped from the text between the first and second iterations.
The final Antalya pact – that was rejected – did, however, retain wording on deforestation agreed by countries in the global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai.
The same draft also “recognises” the role of nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches as “essential climate solutions” – although many experts reject the former term and warn that its vagueness leaves it open to deliberate misuse.
The final draft cover decision “emphasised the importance” of nature, forests, the ocean and other ecosystems as “natural infrastructure for resilience”, while “recogni[sing] that they play a critical role as sinks and reservoirs of greenhouse gases”.
Experts, however, were concerned that this language preceded a paragraph “welcoming” carbon dioxide removal, even if it “stressed” that these methods – that include tree planting – “should ensure environmental safeguards and respect the rights of Indigenous peoples”.
None of the iterations of the rejected cover decision mentioned COP17, the biodiversity summit held in Armenia, which concluded just 10 days before COP31 started. Nor did they mention the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), a landmark pact sealed in 2022 to reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
When Carbon Brief pointed this out to Guilbeault – a key architect of the GBF – in an interview on 17 November, he vowed that he would try to make the case to ministers to get these aspects added in.
One observer told Carbon Brief that the “toxic” nature of discussions over the need for closer “synergies” between climate and biodiversity summits could explain the lack of mentions in the cover decision.
Despite this, they said the rejected pact did “underline” the “urgent need to address, in a comprehensive and synergetic manner, the interlinked global crises of climate change, biodiversity loss, desertification and land and ocean degradation”.
Adopting such language would have represented positive progress, the observer added.
Although the first draft of the cover decision referenced “food” twice – in the context of food security – both of these instances were removed in the subsequent draft. The rejected final cover decision draft mentioned “food security” four times.
However, observers told Carbon Brief that a mention of “food” or “food systems” in the cover decision was not a priority for them. Teresa Anderson, global climate-justice lead at ActionAid, said:
“What we often find is that getting references or language to things in the cover decision doesn’t really play out as impacts on the ground and it’s more effective to push a meaningful agenda in a negotiation space.”
Agriculture and food security
For the second year in a row, negotiations on the Sharm el-Sheikh joint work on agriculture (SJWA) collapsed without parties reaching an agreement.
SJWA is where formal negotiations around climate change and agriculture take place under the UNFCCC.
Part of SJWA’s mandate is to synthesise information about work being done in the agricultural space – under both the UNFCCC and other international bodies – in an annual report.
SJWA also held two workshops – one on holistic approaches to agriculture and one on “means of implementation”, usually taken to mean finance – where countries and other partners could share their experiences, as captured in summary reports.
At COP31, parties were meant to discuss the conclusions of these reports and, time permitting, decide on the future of the agricultural workstream under the UNFCCC. (The four-year mandate of SJWA was set to end at COP31.)
Work “moved very slowly” in the first week, said Oliver Camp, senior policy and implementation specialist at the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition. He added:
“It took a really long time to get into any substantive conversation.”
Ahead of the summit, many observers were hopeful of agreeing a text that recognised agroecology as beneficial for humans, climate and biodiversity.
However, in the first negotiating session, on 10 November, the Arab group expressed its view that fertilisers are vital for food security and fertiliser exports are being impacted by the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM). Therefore, it said, the agriculture talks needed to discuss CBAM and other trade measures.
Teresa Anderson, global climate-justice lead at ActionAid, called this a “total curveball” in the negotiations. She told Carbon Brief:
“Everybody’s faces just dropped…Suddenly we knew that the chances of agroecology having a chance had been pretty elegantly spiked by putting in this really complicated political issue into the middle of the agriculture discussions.”
Other observers also expressed frustration to Carbon Brief that the group had brought CBAM into the negotiations, noting that trade measures are being discussed elsewhere in the COP. (In the end, trade measures were not included in any agreed elements of COP31.)
At the end of this session, parties were asked to submit their views in writing for consideration, with the like-minded developing countries (LMDCs) proposing an extension of SJWA to COP32.
Another major point of contention in the room was what, exactly, a draft text should cover.
The EU – along with Canada – said that the discussion should focus on the commonalities in countries’ positions, rather than the differences. Carbon Brief understands that opposition to this came from the G77 and China, along with the Arab group and the LMDCs, who said that areas of disagreement needed to be addressed through negotiation.
At the same time, said Camp, “there are a few fundamental rifts” around the scope of the work being done in SJWA itself. He told Carbon Brief:
“[There is] this idea that work on agriculture and food security should be primarily focused on adaptation, which is a view held generally by India [and the] G77 and China. Whereas others think it should definitely be led by adaptation, but that there are mitigation co-benefits and that we could take a more comprehensive and holistic view to seek out those co-benefits.”

India's informal economy grows at record pace in Jul-Sep, but paid job creation lags
The number of establishments rose 18.81 per cent from a year earlier to 9.47 crore, while employment increased 16.86 per cent to 15.03 crore, the National Statistics Office (NSO) said in its latest Quarterly Bulletin of the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises. Both growth rates were the highest in the quarterly series.
The composition of employment, however, presents a more mixed picture. The number of hired workers increased by only about 5 per cent to 3.49 crore, while working owners accounted for nearly 62 per cent of the workforce, up from 59.98 per cent a year earlier.
The figures suggest that the expansion of India's vast small-business economy is translating more rapidly into self-employment and owner-operated enterprises than into conventional wage-paying jobs.
Growth was broad-based across rural and urban areas, although urban establishments expanded faster. The number of urban enterprises increased 22.05 per cent year-on-year, compared with 16.05 per cent in rural areas. Employment growth, however, was marginally stronger in rural areas at 17.52 per cent, against 16.30 per cent in urban centres.
Services recorded the strongest expansion among the three broad sectors covered by the survey. Establishments in the 'other services' category grew 29 per cent, while employment increased by more than 33 per cent.
Trade establishments rose 11.70 per cent, with employment increasing 8.36 per cent. Manufacturing establishments expanded 10.55 per cent, but employment growth was more modest at 3.52 per cent.
Retail trade, repair and maintenance, land transport, personal services and apparel manufacturing were among the fastest-growing activities.
The share of hired workers in total employment declined to 23.22 per cent, while working owners' share increased to 61.99 per cent from 59.98 per cent a year earlier. The number of working owners rose by roughly 21 per cent, based on the published employment shares.
The average number of workers per establishment also declined to 1.59 from 1.61, suggesting that the increase in enterprise numbers has not been accompanied by a corresponding rise in average establishment size.
Women accounted for slightly more than 31 per cent of the workforce, compared with 28.70 per cent a year earlier, indicating an increase in their participation in the unincorporated non-farm sector.
The survey also pointed to greater formalisation and digital adoption among unincorporated enterprises.
The share of establishments registered with at least one government or other authority increased to 43.28 per cent from 37.20 per cent a year earlier. Around 80 per cent of establishments reported using cashless payment methods, while nearly 84 per cent used the internet for business purposes.
The NSO, however, noted that questions relating to technology adoption had been redesigned in the latest round, including the introduction of a separate question on online banking and payment gateways, which could affect comparability with previous estimates.
The latest estimates come from a quarterly sample of 1,80,025 establishments spread across 6,002 survey units, substantially smaller than the sample used for the annual survey.
The survey covers unincorporated manufacturing, trade and services enterprises but excludes construction. Its estimates therefore provide a picture of a specific segment of the economy and should not be interpreted as a direct measure of overall GDP or economy-wide employment growth.
Launched in 2021-22, the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises has become an important source of information on businesses operating outside the corporate sector. Quarterly bulletins have been published since 2025.
The latest annual survey, covering calendar 2025, estimated 7.92 crore establishments and 12.81 crore workers, broadly in line with the July-September 2025 quarterly estimates of 7.97 crore establishments and 12.86 crore workers. PTI

DRDO taps Pune startup olee.space for jam-proof laser links to drones
The contract to develop optical communication terminals comes after radio jamming in the Russia-Ukraine war forced drones to rely on fibre-optic tethers for secure communication
Listen to This Article
Pune-based deeptech company olee.space has been awarded a contract by the Defence Research & Development Organisation (DRDO), Ministry of Defence, to develop a laser-link drone communication system. The system will enable secure, high-speed data both ways between ground stations and drones in flight. The company didn’t disclose the contract  value.
In the Russia-Ukraine war, radio jamming became so effective that drones began flying with kilometres of fibre-optic cable trailing behind them just to stay connected. While the cables are immune to jamming, they limit range and can snag or break.
Laser links offer a similar advantage without the tether. Data travels on a narrow beam of light through open air. The result is fibre-like speed, impossible to intercept, and no vulnerability to radio jamming.
Under the contract, olee.space will indigenously design and develop complete ground and airborne Free-Space Optical Communication (FSOC) terminals with automatic Pointing, Acquisition and Tracking (PAT) within 18 months. The system will comprise a tripod-mounted ground terminal with a compact optical payload integrated into a drone, providing a high-bandwidth, full-duplex link over long line-of-sight ranges.
“Holding a laser link on a moving drone is one of the hardest problems in communications, and olee.space is one of very few companies globally working on this capability,” said James Solomon, chief executive officer (CEO) and cofounder, olee.space. “We launched this programme a year ago, and we’re proud to have DRDO’s trust. This is Aatmanirbhar Bharat in action: frontier technology, built in India, competing with the world.”

olee.space is developing laser communication systems for defence, aerospace and critical infrastructure. It handles the entire process in-house, from optical design to field trials, to develop secure, jam-proof laser links for ground, air and space.

ai-4a847676e9.headline: Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the silicon gap with Nvidia
ai-4a847676e9.fulltext:
Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.
The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.
Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.
By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.
In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.
One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.
Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.
In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”
Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”

ai-e1ad855d0e.headline: Tidal bans 100% AI-generated music with plans to delete more than 27m tracks
ai-e1ad855d0e.fulltext:
The music streaming service Tidal has announced it will ban entirely AI-generated music from its platform and remove millions of songs, saying AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans”.
“To ensure Tidal remains the best place for artists to share their work, and for listeners to enjoy it, we’re removing all tracks that we determine are 100% AI generated,” the company announced on Tuesday.
Tracks that were made with assistance from AI will still be allowed but tracks will be rejected if their metadata reveals they were generated solely using AI tools. Tidal’s ban will go into effect on 9 December.
The Norwegian-US streaming service, which promises higher quality audio fidelity as a point of difference from streamers like Apple Music and Spotify, revealed it has seen a huge increase in the number of AI-generated tracks on its platform over the past several months.
In the past 90 days, 43% of tracks distributed on the platform were identified as 100% AI-generated, Tidal said, with 27m songs on the platform – 6.3% – tagged as entirely AI.
On a single day – 6 November – 60% of songs uploaded on a single day were 100% AI.
“Yet Tidal subscribers are not listening to these tracks: 96% of them have received zero streams in the last three months,” the company said, adding that it had taken down 65,000 tracks that were flagged as suspected impersonations of real artists.
“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale,” Tidal said. “It’s true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fanbases. But this situation is different – at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried.”
The company said it would “always fight for artists to get paid more”.
“Everything in this update comes back to that,” the statement said. “If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you.”
Tidal’s policy is the most stridently against AI among all the music streaming services. Bandcamp announced its ban on music “generated wholly or in substantial part by AI” in January. Spotify and Apple Music, the two biggest music streamers, label AI tracks and artists as such but still allow fully generated songs to be distributed on their platforms.
Spotify has promised users a tool to make AI-generated remixes and cover songs but in October it also revealed that it had removed about 50m “slop” tracks from its recommendations to users and outright deleted 75m “spammy” tracks.

ai-d3a6c41efa.headline: Novartis CEO says AI will shave four years off drug development, not cure all disease

Novartis CEO says AI will shave four years off drug development, not cure all disease
Vas Narasimhan, CEO of Swiss drugmaker Novartis and an Anthropic board member, is pushing back on expectations that AI could cure cancer in five to 10 years. That puts him at odds with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and chemistry Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis, who founded DeepMind and its drug discovery spinoff Isomorphic. Around Anthropic's IPO, Amodei suggested that cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, and mental illness could be cured in under a decade, while Hassabis said last year that AI could defeat all diseases within 10 years.
According to the Financial Times, Narasimhan points to a limited understanding of human biology, which is why lengthy animal and human trials will still be needed. His forecast is more cautious: within a decade, he expects AI to cut average drug development only from 12 years to eight, with the early phase before human trials alone accounting for up to two years of that. He also expects success rates in clinical development to rise from 8 percent to 12 percent.
Anthropic is investing in its own drug research, acquired biotech startup Coefficient Bio, and is building a biology lab. Isomorphic raised $5 billion last week and is working with pharmaceutical companies including Novartis on new drugs. Narasimhan sees AI's real benefit as "somewhere in the middle" between ambitious AI forecasts and a skeptical pharma industry.

deep-tech-4329e67e11.headline: India's First Industry-Built PSLV Set For Q1 2027 Launch: ISRO
deep-tech-4329e67e11.fulltext:
India’s first PSLV fully manufactured by the private industry is expected to be launched in the first quarter of 2027, ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan said. The HAL-L&T consortium is building five PSLV rockets under an ₹860 crore contract awarded by NSIL, marking a major step towards industry-led launch vehicle production.
Key Highlights
- India’s first fully industry-built PSLV is expected to launch in Q1 2027.
- HAL and L&T consortium is manufacturing five PSLV rockets under an ₹860 crore NSIL contract.
- ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan said the Gaganyaan orbital module has entered its final stages of development.
- ISRO is seeking greater private-sector participation to expand India’s communication and earth observation satellite capabilities.
India’s First Industry-Built PSLV to Launch in Q1 2027
New Delhi, Nov 25: India’s first Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) to be fully manufactured by the domestic industry is expected to undertake its maiden launch in the first quarter of 2027, Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) Chairman V. Narayanan said on Tuesday.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the India International Space Conclave in New Delhi, Narayanan said the rocket is being manufactured by a consortium of Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and Larsen & Toubro (L&T) under a contract awarded by NewSpace India Limited (NSIL), ISRO’s commercial arm.
He said the consortium had been entrusted with the production of five PSLV rockets and that the first vehicle was getting ready for launch.
“Earlier it was built only by ISRO through the support of the industry, but now the L&T and HAL consortium has been given five PSLVs and the rocket is getting ready. The first launch is expected next year in the first quarter,” Narayanan said.
The five-rocket production contract is valued at ₹860 crore.
HAL-L&T Consortium to Manufacture Five PSLV Rockets
The transfer of PSLV manufacturing to the HAL-L&T consortium is part of the government’s broader strategy to expand private-sector participation in India’s space programme.
Under the arrangement, Indian industry will take on a larger role in manufacturing launch vehicles, enabling ISRO to focus on research, development and advanced space missions while strengthening domestic industrial capabilities.
The initiative also reflects the growing importance of public-private collaboration in meeting India’s expanding launch requirements and strengthening its position in the global space economy.
PSLV: ISRO’s Workhorse Launch Vehicle
The PSLV, often described as ISRO’s workhorse launch vehicle, is an expendable medium-lift rocket weighing approximately 320 tonnes.
Since its first flight in 1993, the launch vehicle has established a strong reliability record and has been extensively used to deploy Indian and international satellites.
Its capabilities include:
- Carrying payloads of up to 1,750 kg to sun-synchronous polar orbits at an altitude of 600 km.
- Deploying satellites into geosynchronous and geostationary orbits.
- Supporting a wide range of Indian and international satellite launch missions.
The industry’s entry into full-scale PSLV manufacturing is expected to expand India’s capacity to produce launch vehicles and support growing demand for satellite deployment.
Gaganyaan Programme: Orbital Module Enters Final Stages
ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan also provided an update on India’s ambitious Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme, saying that work on the orbital module is progressing and has entered its final stages.
Describing Gaganyaan as a highly technology-intensive mission, he said efforts are underway to prepare the spacecraft for upcoming mission milestones.
His remarks came a day after ISRO astronaut Prasanth B. Nair said several procedures and operational protocols required for the mission are being developed from scratch.
Nair highlighted the need for a comprehensive ecosystem of safety, operational and recovery procedures to ensure astronauts can be sent into space and brought back safely.
The first uncrewed mission, Gaganyaan-1, is expected to carry an AI-enabled half-humanoid robot as ISRO validates spacecraft systems and mission procedures ahead of a crewed flight.
ISRO Seeks Greater Private-Sector Participation in Space Sector
Narayanan also emphasised that India’s expanding space requirements cannot be met by the government sector alone.
He noted that India currently has 56 space assets and will require many more communication and earth observation satellites in the coming years.
“We need to develop a lot of space assets for communication and earth observation. This cannot be done only by the government sector,” he said.
The ISRO Chairman called for stronger collaboration between the space agency and private companies to expand satellite infrastructure, improve manufacturing capabilities and support India’s growing presence in the global space economy.
The planned Q1 2027 launch of India’s first fully industry-built PSLV marks an important milestone in the country’s space-sector reforms. With HAL and L&T manufacturing five launch vehicles under an ₹860 crore contract, India is moving towards greater industrial participation in launch vehicle production. Alongside progress in Gaganyaan, the initiative reflects ISRO’s broader effort to expand national space capabilities through public-private collaboration.

climate-energy-e41a1b1bc8.headline: Govt proposes battery storage for larger rooftop solar systems
climate-energy-e41a1b1bc8.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: Govt has proposed making battery storage mandatory for larger rooftop solar installations, with consumers potentially required to install storage capacity equivalent to at least 20% of their daily generation, as it seeks to address grid management challenges arising from growing adoption of distributed renewable energy.
Under the revised draft Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules, 2026, circulated by the power ministry for stakeholder comments, state electricity regulatory commissions (SERCs) will be empowered to specify the capacity threshold beyond which rooftop solar consumers will have to install energy storage systems. In the absence of a threshold, the requirement will apply to renewable energy installations exceeding 10 kW.
The proposed provision will come into effect from April 1, 2028. Officials said the move is aimed at encouraging consumers to store surplus solar power generated during the day for use during evening peak hours, reducing the pressure on distribution companies (discoms) to manage fluctuations in renewable energy generation and procure expensive power to meet peak demand.
The ministry has also proposed changes to the net-metering framework, allowing SERCs to levy charges on rooftop solar consumers beyond a specified capacity threshold, taking into account the imputed cost of energy storage and network losses. 
No such charges will be levied up to the capacity threshold determined by the respective commission.
Officials said rooftop solar consumers use the distribution network to inject surplus power during solar hours and draw electricity during non-solar hours without fully contributing to the recovery of fixed costs. “It results in increased cross-subsidisation by other retail consumers. We have tried to address this issue,” said an official.
The draft also proposes allowing consumers to install renewable energy generation systems on other parts of their premises apart from rooftops, with installed capacity permitted to exceed their sanctioned electricity load, subject to limits prescribed by SERCs.
Govt has also proposed deferring the implementation of time-of-day tariffs to April 1, 2028, for consumers with maximum demand exceeding 10 kW and April 1, 2029, for other non-agricultural consumers.
The draft also seeks to strengthen consumer protection by requiring discoms to automatically review unusually high or low electricity bills, where consumption exceeds five times or falls below one-fifth of the average consumption during the previous six billing cycles. Consumers will not face disconnection if they continue paying based on their average consumption until the discrepancy is resolved, which must be done within 30 days.

climate-energy-3847272664.headline: India’s solar power capacity addition may surpass 2025 record in current year
climate-energy-3847272664.fulltext:
Updated - November 23, 2026  at 09:11 PM.
| 
         New Delhi
     India’s annual solar power installed capacity in 2026 calendar year is expected to surpass the record deployment of 38 gigawatts (GW) achieved in 2025, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said.
Solar power installed capacity in India tripled between 2020 and 2025 to about 140 GW, with annual additions reaching a record 38 GW in 2025, the agency said.
Between January and August 2026, India installed 32 GW, which was supported by record auction volumes in 2024 and developers rushing to commission projects ahead of new domestic sourcing requirements for solar PV cells coming fully into effect, it added.
“Annual deployment is therefore expected to reach a new record in 2026, followed by a short-term slowdown due to lower auction volumes in 2025 and 2026,” IEA noted.
By 2030, India’s solar PV capacity is expected to increase by a factor of 2.5, exceeding 350 GW, which is supported by strong cost competitiveness, sustained auction activity, growing demand through open access mechanisms and accelerating deployment of rooftop solar.
Utility-scale projects have accounted for around 75 per cent of the solar PV capacity additions over the last 5 years. Their share is expected to gradually decline to around 70 per cent by 2030 as policy support, improving economics and simplified administrative procedures accelerate growth in the distributed segment, the IEA anticipated.
The IEA noted that competitive auctions have been a key enabling mechanism for utility-scale projects, supporting transparent price discovery, lowering procurement costs and facilitating large-scale capacity deployment.
Since 2010, India has awarded around 220 GW of utility-scale renewable capacity through this mechanism, with a record 60 GW allocated in 2024. In 2025, average auction tariffs for newly commissioned solar PV projects were around 40 per cent lower than the average cost of the coal-fired electricity supply.
In recent years, auction design has evolved from technology-specific tenders towards more sophisticated formats requiring hybrid projects that combine solar PV, wind power and energy storage to deliver firmer and more dispatchable electricity supply.
The agency pointed out that the solar park model further accelerated deployment by reducing risks associated with land acquisition, permitting and grid connection, while the Green Energy Corridor programme has expanded transmission infrastructure to facilitate the evacuation of renewable electricity from resource-rich regions.
Open-access procurement — direct power contracting between consumers and generators — has also become an increasingly important source of demand for utility-scale renewable energy, particularly among commercial and industrial consumers seeking to reduce electricity costs and meet corporate sustainability targets.
Open-access renewable projects have become an important complement to government-led procurement programmes, particularly in States with high industrial electricity demand such as Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan. About 7 GW of solar PV and wind capacity was contracted through open access in 2025, the IEA said.

indian-startups-46058dffd2.headline: Sarvam AI Launches Dictation API For English, 22 Indian Languages
indian-startups-46058dffd2.fulltext: AI unicorn Sarvam AI has launched Sarvam Dictate, an API that lets developers add voice dictation in English and 22 Indian languages to their applications. Priced at ₹0.50 per minute of audio, the service combines speech recognition with transcript editing in a single API call. It is designed to turn spoken inputs into text for messages, documents, and business records. Dictate pairs the startup’s Saaras V4 speech recognition model with a version of its Sarvam 105B large language model trained for dictation. The first transcribes the audio, while the second edits the resulting text. Announcing the launch on X, Sarvam claimed that Dictate outperformed Google's Gemini 3.5 Transcribe and AssemblyAI Dictation on a set of real-world dictation tests. According to the startup, for English dictations of up to one minute, the API required 40% fewer character edits than Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. Across Indian languages and Hinglish, the reduction stood at 47%. For longer English dictations, Dictate required 11% fewer character edits than Gemini and 17% fewer than AssemblyAI. Sarvam highlighted that its Dictate API is designed to account for the way people naturally speak, and can handle speakers switching between English and Indian languages mid-sentence, correcting themselves, and making false starts. It also cleans up pauses and repetitions to produce a more refined transcript. Developers can provide up to 1,000 names and technical terms per request, alongside contextual information such as customer relationship management (CRM) records, product lists, and a description of the situation. They can also specify formatting preferences and choose how Indian languages and English appear in the output, including native scripts or Latin letters. The API supports live dictation and uploaded recordings of up to an hour, returning both the raw transcript and edited text. Its documented applications include chat messages, sales records, forms, and meeting minutes. As per Sarvam, Dictate has already been tested through Kivi, its dictation application, where users have dictated more than 30 Mn words since launch. Voice AI Gains Ground The launch comes as AI developers increasingly integrate voice interfaces into applications for documentation, customer interactions, and data entry. Potential uses span customer support, telehealth, medical documentation, and sales record updates, extending the scope for Sarvam’s multilingual voice AI offerings. India’s linguistic diversity presents a significant opportunity for voice AI, with the domestic market projected to reach $1.8 Bn by 2030, according to Nasscom. Startups are developing speech-to-text models to tap this demand for multilingual applications. Earlier today, voice AI infrastructure startup Murf AI launched Finch, a streaming speech-to-text model that it claims ranks first across 11 Indian languages on the Voice of India benchmark, ahead of models from ElevenLabs, OpenAI, xAI, and Microsoft. Murf claims Finch delivers a time-to-final-segment of 50 milliseconds and supports code-mixed speech and optional voice isolation. Sarvam’s latest launch also follows the rollout of Token Factory, a platform that gives enterprises API access to its own models alongside global open-weight models, including Google’s Gemma and China’s DeepSeek. Token Factory drew questions over whether Sarvam had used government-subsidised GPU capacity allocated for developing homegrown models to host foreign models. The startup subsequently clarified that the platform runs on privately procured GPUs. Reiterating its focus on model development, Sarvam said it will launch more models across vision, speech, and edge AI over the next two weeks.

The test firing of JWALA MK-1—having a 5-km operational range and designed as a domestically built, autonomous and affordable counter-drone solution—was carried out Monday at Pokhran, Rajasthan.
The test at Pokhran highlights the role of private manufacturers in India’s defence sector. As the country pursues defence indigenisation, indigenous missiles, autonomous systems and AI-powered battle management platforms are expected to contribute to national security.
The development comes after the expanding use of inexpensive attack drones in conflicts and the challenge of intercepting them with costly conventional air-defence systems.
The imbalance cost can pressure interceptor inventories, ammunition supplies and the economics of air defence. Given India’s current security environment, developing cost-friendly and scalable counter-drone technology is a strategic priority, the defence firm said.

“India needs indigenous, reliable and cost-effective solutions to counter emerging aerial threats at scale,” he said.
Sharma presented JWALA MK-1 as a step towards an integrated counter-drone capability combining technology, mission autonomy and operational effectiveness. He said indigenous systems were important for strengthening India’s preparedness for battlefield challenges and advancing defence self-reliance.

india-deep-tech-4843abea01.headline: Indian Navy, Coast Guard to purchase 76 naval utility helicopters

New Delhi: In a proposal expected to be worth around Rs 15,000 Crore, the Indian Navy and the Indian Coast Guard are looking to place orders for 76 utility helicopters, which would replace their vintage fleet of Cheetah/Chetak light choppers.
As per the plan, the Indian Navy would acquire 51 of these utility helicopters while the Coast Guard will get 25 of them. The programme would see Indian firms partnering with foreign OEMs to manufacture the choppers within India under Make in India, defence sources told ANI.
The project is expected to be taken up for discussion at a very high-level Defence Ministry meeting very soon and will be under the Buy and Make (Indian) category of the Defence Acquisition Procedure, they said.
The two forces are planning to induct the 5-tonne-plus class choppers at a time when the forces have faced issues with their existing fleet of twin-engine choppers, the sources said.
The choppers are being acquired by the forces as part of larger efforts by the three defence forces to replace their fleet of vintage choppers, as the Indian Army and the Air Force are also looking at buying 400 light choppers, of which 200 would be made by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, while the remaining 200 would be made by private sector companies in partnership with foreign OEMs.
The programme for the 200 light choppers to be built by the private sector firms was cleared recently by the Defence Acquisition Council, and a tender is expected to be issued soon.

The United States has added Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed International, which is at the centre of an alleged Nvidia chip-smuggling and espionage scandal, to its trade blacklist, tightening restrictions on its access to American technology.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which operates under the Department of Commerce, on Monday placed Megaspeed International and six other companies in Southeast Asia on its Entity List, citing concerns that they were acting contrary to US national security or foreign policy interests.
The move comes amid an intensifying investigation into allegations that Megaspeed diverted high-end Nvidia chips to China in violation of US export controls. The company has been under investigation by the US Department of Justice.
Quick answers to key questions
•5 QUESTIONS
1
Why did the US blacklist Megaspeed International?⌵
US officials cited concerns that Megaspeed and related entities could divert advanced computing technology to unauthorised users or uses. The action is linked to an investigation into alleged transfers of Nvidia AI chips to China in possible violation of US export controls.
2
What does Megaspeed’s addition to the US Entity List mean?⌵
Companies and individuals seeking to supply Megaspeed with advanced American technology, including high-end Nvidia GPUs, must obtain an export licence from the US government.
3
Which companies were blacklisted alongside Megaspeed?⌵
The other named entities were MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, Swiftdata and Megaspeed (Thailand). They are based in Singapore, Malaysia or Thailand.
4
Did Megaspeed illegally divert Nvidia chips to China?⌵
That has not been established in the provided reports. The alleged diversion is under investigation, and Megaspeed has rejected the allegations, calling itself a legitimate and lawful business.
5
Are investigations into Megaspeed still ongoing?⌵
Yes. The US investigation concerns alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China, while Singapore is examining whether Megaspeed may have breached local laws.
In its filing to the Federal Register, BIS identified seven entities across Southeast Asia, including three firms based in Malaysia, two in Singapore and one in Thailand, in addition to Megaspeed International.
The other companies named were MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, Swiftdata and Megaspeed (Thailand).
The blacklisting means that companies and individuals seeking to supply these entities with advanced American technology, including Nvidia's high-end graphics processing units (GPUs) used to power artificial intelligence systems, will need to obtain an export licence from the US government.
Megaspeed has previously rejected allegations surrounding its operations, describing itself as a "legitimate and lawful business" and arguing that media reports contained claims that were not supported by verifiable evidence.
US officials have accused Alice Huang, Megaspeed International's former senior executive, of working with China's Ministry of State Security in an intelligence-gathering operation targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
The allegations are based on US intelligence reports first reported by The New York Times. Beijing has rejected the claims. Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the allegations.
The developments come on the same day that Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO in a dramatic comeback that triggered a sharp rally in technology stocks.
In a social media post, Trump said the Nvidia board had made the "correct and proper decision" and argued that the United States needed Huang's leadership to ensure the success of the company and the broader American economy.
"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," Trump said.
He added that the US Attorney General had confirmed that the government did not possess evidence that Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct.
However, Trump also called on Nvidia to continue its internal investigation into compliance with US export controls, stressing that the company had a legal and national security responsibility to ensure its obligations were met.

According to Moneycontrol, Pixxel has outlined an ambitious phased expansion plan for the proposed manufacturing facility, with the capacity to produce multiple satellites simultaneously. "We expect to have the capacity to build 50 satellites in parallel by mid-2027, scaling to 100 by the end of 2027 and to 200 by mid-2028," the company said in a statement, as reported by Moneycontrol. The facility is expected to become operational in 2027, with manufacturing capacity increasing in phases. The project marks an important step in Pixxel's efforts to move towards large-scale satellite manufacturing rather than operating at a relatively limited production capacity. Pixxel's decision to establish the facility in Bengaluru comes after a period of competition among southern states to attract the company. His remarks prompted competing pitches from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, each seeking to attract the spacetech company's proposed manufacturing investment. Karnataka's existing aerospace and space research ecosystem appears to have strengthened its position. Kharge pointed to the state's established institutional and industrial base, highlighting the presence of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), key Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) centres, leading spacetech companies and an extensive space-sector supply chain. He also highlighted the state's SpaceTech Policy 2025-30, which aims to develop dedicated space manufacturing clusters and common testing facilities. According to Moneycontrol, these initiatives are part of Karnataka's broader push to strengthen its position in space research, manufacturing and innovation. Pixxel has emerged as one of India's prominent private spacetech companies, with its six-satellite Firefly constellation already in orbit. The company has also reportedly secured contracts with the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), expanding its presence in the international space market. It was also selected to lead a consortium tasked with developing India's first privately led national Earth-observation constellation, comprising 12 satellites. The GigaPixxel facility is expected to support these ambitions by giving the company greater control over satellite production and the infrastructure required to scale its operations. The proposed manufacturing unit is another boost to Bengaluru's position as a major centre for India's aerospace and space industry. The city already hosts key space research institutions, defence establishments, technology companies and a network of suppliers supporting the aerospace sector. The addition of a large-scale private satellite manufacturing facility could further strengthen this ecosystem. For Karnataka, the investment also aligns with its broader strategy to attract private-sector participation in space manufacturing, research and innovation. As satellite-based services gain importance across areas such as agriculture, climate monitoring, disaster management and national security, demand for Earth-observation capabilities is expected to create opportunities for companies across the space value chain. GigaPixxel's planned expansion represents not just a manufacturing investment for Pixxel but also a significant development in Bengaluru's ambition to become a major destination for commercial satellite production. india-2f9bcfe39f.headline: Why has the FSSAI sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri? | Explained
india-2f9bcfe39f.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-2f9bcfe39f.fulltext:
The story so far: On November 22, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the country’s apex food-safety regulator, sanctioned prosecution against packaged drinking water manufacturer Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd. after a sample of its water was found to be non-compliant with prescribed safety standards, with the regulator declaring it unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
The public-health stakes are significant. In 2023, bottled water was the principal source of drinking water for 15% of urban and 6% of rural households, as per Data For India. For consumers buying it at railway stations, airports, highway eateries and neighbourhood shops, a sealed bottle is often taken as an assurance of safety. Yet, the data submitted in Parliament in February 2025 revealed that 333 of 1,300 enforcement samples of packaged drinking water tested in 2023-24 failed to meet prescribed standards. Similarly, in 2022-23, 650 of 1,776 samples had been found non-compliant.
According to the FSSAI, a sample of packaged drinking water (other than mineral water) collected from Bisleri’s premises was found to be non-compliant with the prescribed limits for “bromate” and was declared unsafe under the 2006 Act. Following an appeal by the food business operator (FBO), the sample was referred to a Referral Food Laboratory for further examination, which also declared the sample unsafe, citing the detection of “polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons” (PAHs).
In its response, Bisleri has maintained that its water is safe for consumption, saying the matter concerned a batch manufactured at its Goa facility in September 2025, one of 143 manufacturing plants in its network. In a statement issued on November 23, the company said the FSSAI had collected six samples from its Goa facility on September 30, 2025. While five samples met the prescribed standards, the sixth recorded a “bromate” level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre. Further, Bisleri said it appealed on November 22, 2025, following which the sample was sent to a referral laboratory for retesting. The laboratory, as claimed, found the bromate level within the prescribed limit but separately detected PAHs. Citing the divergent test findings, the company reportedly arranged an independent examination of the same sample at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, which, according to Bisleri, also found the bromate level within limits. The company said it submitted these results to FSSAI’s Western Regional Office on February 2, 2026, but received no further communication and understood that the matter had been closed.
Water is essential for digestion, blood circulation, temperature regulation and kidney function, but its safety cannot be judged by its appearance, taste, odour or sealed packaging alone. Contamination may be microbiological, causing illnesses such as diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid, or chemical, with some substances posing risks through prolonged exposure. In India, packaged water broadly falls into two categories: (1) “packaged drinking water”, which may be sourced from surface water, groundwater or seawater and treated through processes such as filtration, decantation, reverse osmosis (RO) and disinfection; and (2) “natural mineral water”, drawn from protected underground sources and characterised by a relatively stable mineral composition. Both must meet prescribed chemical and microbiological safety standards.

world-0073f74c97.headline: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
world-0073f74c97.fulltext:
China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
- Published
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."
