science-mind-f82e2058d3.headline: Many languages, one common neural code
science-mind-f82e2058d3.fulltext:
Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.
Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way.
Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study published today in Nature Neuroscience, the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages.
“Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says Evelina Fedorenko, who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper.
The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing.
Parsing the linguistic mind
Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere.
“Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center.
While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way.
For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker?
It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence.
Where AI meets the brain
Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing lens into the human mind. Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope.
“Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach.
Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input.
Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages.
A mental bridge between languages
The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages.
“We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.”
Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication.
What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko.
In science, this new study gives brain researchers some explanations for long-held curiosities among them. In society, it could steer emerging technologies into a more inclusive direction. Scientists are starting to explore clinical uses of AI language tools, such as those that can detect cognitive decline based on brain activity patterns during language. But most of those studies, and the methods clinicians use today, are in common and well-studied languages like English. By showing how AI and the human brain overlap across many diverse languages, this new research may be a step toward clinical tools that do not leave most speakers out.
In another vein, reversing the Fedorenko lab’s approach might help preserve languages on the brink of extinction. “Say you had one single speaker of a language that is dying out. You might imagine a case in which we can train a model in the opposite direction: give it images of that speaker’s brain, and it could translate those into language,” notes Fedorenko.
De Varda adds that there are features that clearly differ between languages, too, and that those must be somehow represented in the brain and even LLMs. Defining those differences in future research, he says, might unearth new fragments of knowledge to complete the puzzle of the linguistic mind.

science-mind-082cb587f7.headline: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
science-mind-082cb587f7.fulltext:
New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
- Date:
  November 24, 2026
- Source:
  University of Sydney
- Summary:
  A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals. The treatment also prevented severe memory decline in mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Remarkably, the approach relies on mRNA technology similar to that used in COVID-19 vaccines.
The discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a new path toward treating conditions that affect the brain. Potential applications extend beyond Alzheimer's disease to other neurodegenerative disorders, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental conditions.
"If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely said.
The idea behind the research has an unusual origin. The team drew inspiration from Daniel Keyes' science fiction story Flowers for Algernon, which explores the limits of human intelligence through experiments designed to increase intelligence in laboratory mice and people.
How mRNA Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory
The treatment works by delivering messenger RNA (mRNA), a type of genetic instruction that tells cells how to produce specific proteins. These instructions are enclosed in tiny fat-based particles called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which protect the mRNA and help it enter cells.
Once delivered through the nose, the mRNA instructs cells to manufacture therapeutic proteins capable of reaching the brain. In effect, the nasal tissue becomes a small drug-producing factory, creating substances that can support brain function.
"In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime," Professor Neely said.
"What's exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic."
The study, published in Advanced Science, used mRNA to stimulate production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). This naturally occurring protein helps neurons survive, form connections, and adapt as the brain learns and stores memories. Levels of BDNF tend to decline with aging and are also associated with Alzheimer's disease.
The results were striking. Older mice that received the nose drops performed about as well as young mice in standardized tests of working memory, spatial memory, and object recognition. These tests measure abilities such as remembering recently encountered information, navigating surroundings, and recognizing familiar objects. Untreated older animals showed the expected age-related deterioration in cognitive performance.
Nose Drops Prevent Alzheimer's-Like Memory Decline in Mice
To investigate whether the treatment might also protect against Alzheimer's disease, researchers turned to a widely used laboratory model known as 5XFAD mice. These animals carry genetic mutations that cause them to develop Alzheimer's-like brain changes and memory problems unusually early in life.
In this model, signs of Alzheimer's-related brain pathology can typically be detected by two months of age, with measurable cognitive decline appearing around four months.
The researchers began administering the BDNF-producing mRNA nose drops when the mice were two months old, around the time the disease-related changes first appeared. Treatment continued twice a week.
By four months of age, the treated mice showed no further cognitive decline, unlike the severe deterioration normally seen in this model. The findings suggest that supporting brain cells early in the disease process may help preserve cognitive abilities.
One of the most intriguing results was what the treatment did not do. Although memory and learning were protected, the researchers found no reduction in amyloid plaques, the abnormal protein deposits that accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease.
That distinction could be important because many existing Alzheimer's treatments aim to remove amyloid. The new approach instead appears to help neurons remain healthy and functional despite the presence of these deposits. If the same effect can eventually be demonstrated in people, the two treatment strategies might be used together.
"Current Alzheimer's treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques," Professor Neely said. "However, just under a third of Alzheimer's patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it's possible to live with Alzheimer's disease pathology."
"Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other."
Bypassing the Blood-Brain Barrier Through the Nose
Getting medicines into the brain is one of the biggest obstacles in developing treatments for neurological diseases. The blood-brain barrier acts as a protective filter, preventing many potentially harmful substances in the bloodstream from entering delicate brain tissue. Unfortunately, it also blocks numerous drugs that scientists would like to use to treat brain disorders.
The nose offers a possible alternative route. Connections between the nasal cavity and the central nervous system may allow certain therapeutic substances to reach the brain without requiring surgery or injections directly into the brain or spinal cord.
"This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose," Professor Neely said.
The team adapted mRNA technology built on the same clinically validated BioNTech platform used for COVID-19 vaccination. Instead of delivering instructions that prompt an immune response, the modified system provides instructions for producing proteins intended to benefit the brain.
First author Dr. Maria Bergamasco, from the University of Sydney's School of Life and Environmental Sciences, explained that the findings illustrate how mRNA technology could be used for purposes far beyond preventing infectious diseases.
"The success of mRNA vaccines showed these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells," Dr. Bergamasco said.
"We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way."
Treatment Stimulates New Brain Cell Growth
The researchers also detected increased neurogenesis, the process through which new neurons are formed, in the hippocampus. This part of the brain plays an essential role in learning and memory and is particularly vulnerable to damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.
The increase in new neurons provides another possible explanation for the improvements in cognitive performance. By promoting the health and adaptability of brain cells, BDNF may help maintain the neural networks needed for learning and remembering information.
The nose drops also appeared to be well tolerated. Researchers reported no major side effects in the mice during the study, although further testing will be needed to establish long-term safety.
Could mRNA Nose Drops Work in Humans?
Despite the encouraging results, Professor Neely emphasized that the treatment remains experimental. So far, its effectiveness has been demonstrated only in mice, and additional animal safety studies are required before clinical testing can begin.
"Before we can trial this therapy in patients, we need to perform a series of safety studies in animals," he said. "It is a very promising pathway, but human noses are different from mouse noses, so we will need to test our drugs in humans before we know whether it will work."
That anatomical difference is a significant consideration. A delivery method that successfully transports therapeutic substances from the nasal cavity to the brain in mice may not work in exactly the same way in humans.
Nevertheless, the researchers believe the potential applications could be substantial. Beyond protecting against Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline, the technology might eventually help support memory and other mental abilities during normal aging.
"We believe our new drug, if it works in humans, can promote general cognitive health as people age, should help treat a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, and may even increase cognitive abilities in healthy young people," Professor Neely said.
The next steps involve refining the nasal delivery technology and conducting further studies to determine its safety and effectiveness over longer periods. The team hopes to advance toward human clinical trials as quickly as the required testing allows.
"Based on previous clinical trials, we know the components used in this study to be safe in humans," Professor Neely said. "We hope we can move quickly through the requisite safety studies and trial this treatment in humans in the next two years."
Although the individual components have previously been used in humans, the complete nasal treatment still requires its own safety evaluation. Whether it can deliver similar memory benefits in people remains an open question.
Research Funding and Disclosures
The project brought together researchers from the Dr. John and Anne Chong Lab for Functional Genomics in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences, the Charles Perkins Centre, and the University of Sydney's Faculty of Medicine and Health.
Greg Neely and Maria Bergamasco are listed as inventors on a provisional patent application associated with the research. The other authors reported no competing interests.
Financial support came from the National Health and Medical Research Council, the NSW Ministry of Health, and an ongoing philanthropic contribution from Dr. John and Anne Chong supporting the Neely Lab's research. The authors also acknowledged the Sydney Imaging Facility for its assistance.
All animal experiments were approved by the University of Sydney Animal Ethics Committee and conducted in accordance with the Australian Code of Practise for the Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes.

science-mind-14fcda5481.headline: Psilocybin and Ketamine Break Rigid Habits to Improve Decision-Making
science-mind-14fcda5481.fulltext:
Summary:
New neuroscience research reveals that both psilocybin and ketamine improve decision accuracy by helping the brain rely less on rigid, repetitive habits and more on real-time sensory cues. The study shows that rather than scrambling neural signaling, these compounds gently sculpt ongoing brain activity, trading a slight reduction in reaction speed for sharper, more flexible choices.
Key Facts:
- Breaking Repetitive Habits: Mice treated with either psilocybin or ketamine made significantly fewer mistakes during a light-guided reward task, overcoming the habitual bias to repeat previous choices in favor of current sensory evidence.
- Subtle Sculpting Over Chaos: Brain-wide genetic mapping and neural recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex revealed that psilocybin induces widespread yet subtle shifts, preserving task-related activity patterns while gently fine-tuning how the brain updates beliefs.
- The Speed-Accuracy Tradeoff: While decision accuracy improved markedly following psychedelic treatment, mice took slightly longer to make their choices, highlighting a speed-accuracy tradeoff relevant to real-world safety and therapeutic dosing.
Source: Boston University
For the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s. Conventional antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) often require weeks to take effect, demand chronic daily use, and fail to provide adequate relief for roughly 30% of patients with treatment-resistant depression.
Against this backdrop, psychedelic compounds, including classic serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin and dissociative agents like ketamine, have sparked intense clinical excitement for their ability to produce rapid, durable improvements in mood, addiction, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Yet precisely how these drugs alter neural circuits to break entrenched patterns of negative thinking has remained poorly understood.
Now, in a study published in Science Advances, neuroscientists at Boston University led by assistant professor Dr. Benjamin Scott and associate professor Dr. Steve Ramirez have uncovered a shared pro-cognitive mechanism linking psilocybin and ketamine: both drugs weaken the brain’s reliance on automatic habits and heighten sensitivity to immediate sensory cues.
Overriding Habitual Bias With Sensory Evidence
To test how psychedelics influence moment-to-moment decision-making, Scott, Ramirez, and colleagues trained mice on a perceptual task requiring the animals to use brief pulses of light to identify which of two ports contained a reward.
Untreated mice performed the task moderately well, but frequently fell into habitual traps—repeatedly returning to a previously rewarded location even when the light cues clearly signaled a change. Following administration of either psilocybin or ketamine, however, mice made significantly fewer errors. Rather than falling back on repetitive choice biases, treated animals anchored their decisions much more closely to real-time sensory information.
“These findings reveal how psychedelics reduce the reliance on habits and repetitive choices, which may explain part of their therapeutic effect,” explained Scott, a faculty member in Boston University’s Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.
Gently Sculpting Orbitofrontal Decision Circuits
Although psilocybin acts primarily on serotonin receptors (such as 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A) while ketamine blocks glutamate NMDA receptors, their behavioral effects converged on sharper, less biased decision-making.
To observe what changed inside the brain, the researchers combined brain-wide genetic activity mapping with targeted neural recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a prefrontal region essential for evaluating rewards, making decisions, and updating beliefs when rules change.
Remarkably, psilocybin did not erase or scramble existing task representations. Instead, core OFC activity patterns tracking sensory cues and choices remained largely intact, accompanied by widespread yet subtle adjustments across interconnected brain regions. According to the authors, this gentle sculpting of ongoing neural activity aligns closely with clinical observations that a person’s mindset and environment (“set and setting”) strongly shape the psychedelic experience.
A Speed-Accuracy Tradeoff and Future Non-Hallucinogenic Targets
The team also identified an important behavioral nuance: while mice made more accurate choices after receiving psilocybin or ketamine, they took longer to deliberate, revealing a classic speed-accuracy tradeoff. While slower deliberation can benefit reflective cognitive therapy, it underscores why activities demanding split-second reaction times, such as driving, are unsafe under the influence of these compounds.
Looking ahead, Scott and Ramirez plan to pinpoint the exact neural pathways responsible for breaking rigid habits, with the ultimate goal of developing targeted, next-generation therapies that unlock cognitive flexibility without hallucinogenic side effects.
Questions and Answers
How do psilocybin and ketamine improve decision-making in this study?
Boston University researchers found that both drugs help the brain pay closer attention to immediate sensory cues (like flashes of light) while reducing the tendency to fall back on repetitive habits, leading to significantly more accurate choices.
Do psychedelics scramble normal brain activity during a task?
No. Recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex showed that the brain’s core patterns for tracking cues and making decisions remained largely preserved. Instead of causing chaos, psilocybin induced widespread yet subtle shifts that gently sculpted how the brain updated its beliefs.
Were there any downsides to the improved decision accuracy?
Yes. Researchers observed a speed-accuracy tradeoff: while treated animals made fewer mistakes, they took longer to make their decisions, suggesting these compounds slow down reaction times even as they promote more deliberative thinking.

- DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeb3041
Abstract
Psychedelics Shift Decision Strategies and Reconfigure Orbitofrontal Dynamics
Psychedelics such as psilocybin and ketamine are attracting renewed attention as rapid-acting therapeutics, yet how they reshape cognitive computations remains poorly understood.
To address this, we trained mice on a free-response perceptual decision-making task that disentangles bias-driven from sensory-guided strategies. Acute administration of psilocybin or ketamine slowed decision times while improving accuracy. Behavioral modeling combining drift diffusion and GLM-HMM approaches revealed that these effects were driven by increased decision thresholds and a shift toward sensory-engaged states.
Whole-brain c-Fos mapping identified modulation of distributed task-related networks, including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Calcium imaging showed that OFC population dynamics were reorganized under psychedelic conditions, with preserved task selectivity but altered temporal structure and shifted population correlations.
Together, these findings indicate that psychedelics shift decision-making toward greater reliance on sensory evidence while reshaping cortical population dynamics, providing a system-level account of their effects on perceptual decisions.

Layoffs and AI fears: 72% of India's tech workers want to switch careers
56% wouldn't steer their kids into tech, and just 4% would recommend software engineering to a young person starting out
Listen to This Article
India's technology sector, long regarded as one of the country's most attractive career destinations for its high salaries and global opportunities, is facing a growing crisis of confidence among its own workforce. As layoffs, restructuring and concerns about artificial intelligence reshape the industry, nearly three out of four technology professionals in India say they would switch to an entirely different career if given the opportunity.
A survey of 2,958 India-based professionals by anonymous workplace community platform Blind found that 72% would leave their current careers for a completely different profession if there were no financial costs or retraining requirements. 72% said they would switch to a completely different career tomorrow if it required no cost or retraining. The largest group, 42%, would make the move as long as the pay stayed the same. Only 13% said they are happy where they are.
While 30% said they would make the switch immediately, another 42% said they would do so if they could retain their existing salaries. Only 13% said they were happy with their current careers and would not consider leaving.
Also Read
The findings point to a growing disconnect between the financial rewards associated with technology jobs and professionals' long-term satisfaction and confidence in the sector.
The reluctance to remain in technology is also extending to the next generation. Around 56% of respondents said they would probably or definitely not encourage their children to pursue careers in tech. Nearly one in three, or 31%, said they would definitely discourage them.
" The urge to leave was strongest at Intuit (89%), Goldman Sachs (87%), PayPal (87%), Visa (86%), Expedia Group (83%). It ran nearly as high at Oracle (79%), which has reportedly cut about 12,000 jobs in India this year, as well as at Salesforce (79%) and Adobe (78%), where Blind users have reported silent layoffs in India. Even at Meta and Apple, where it was lowest, more than half would switch," the company said in a statement. 
The career shift has already shown up on Blind. With more than a month left in the year, posts written in India about leaving software engineering are up 37.5% from all of 2025. For a growing number of India's tech workers, the question is no longer which company to join next, but whether to stay in tech at all.
"They don’t want the next generation pursuing tech, either. 56% said they would definitely or probably not encourage their child to go into tech. Nearly 1 in 3 said definitely not. That view holds even at the companies young Indians most want to join. At Microsoft, the largest group of respondents, 67% would steer their child away from tech, and over 50% felt the same at Google and Amazon," said Blind in a release.
The survey comes amid continued restructuring across the technology industry, with concerns over job security, changing skill requirements and the impact of artificial intelligence influencing career decisions. Blind surveyed 2,958 India-based professionals between November 6 and 19, 2026. Company figures include only companies with at least 10 responses to the question.
Healthcare beats software engineering as preferred career choice
When asked which profession they would recommend to a young person starting out today, respondents showed a clear preference for careers they believe offer greater long-term stability or are less vulnerable to automation.
Medical and healthcare careers emerged as the most preferred option, selected by 34% of respondents.
Artificial intelligence and machine learning came second, with 19%, followed by government and public sector jobs at 15%.
Other technology roles, including data, cybersecurity and hardware, accounted for 10% of responses. Law and finance also received 10%, while arts and teaching were chosen by 8%.
Software engineering ranked last, with just 4% of respondents recommending it as a career choice.
Notably, not a single respondent from Google, Meta or NVIDIA selected software engineering as their preferred career recommendation for young people.
The preference for healthcare and public sector careers suggests that professionals are increasingly weighing factors beyond salary, including job security, resilience to technological disruption and long-term earning potential.
AI creates a career paradox
The survey also highlights an interesting contradiction in how technology workers view artificial intelligence.
While software engineering received only 4% of recommendations, AI and machine learning emerged as the second-most preferred career path, attracting 19% of responses.
This suggests that professionals are not necessarily turning away from technology altogether. Instead, they may be reassessing which technology skills and roles will remain valuable as AI adoption accelerates.
The preference for healthcare, government employment and specialised technology functions also reflects a growing interest in careers perceived to offer more durable opportunities.
Asked which path they would most recommend to someone starting out today, respondents leaned toward work AI cannot easily replace, or into AI itself. Medicine and healthcare led at 34%, and 15% picked government or public sector jobs. AI and machine learning came second at 19%. In a Blind thread on which profession has the highest earning potential over a lifetime in India, an Apple employee replied: "IAS (civil services) followed by IPS. Earn more than politicians, never get voted out." In another thread, a Cisco employee listed hands-on jobs: "Landscaper. Plumber. Hvac technician. Dentist. Veterinarian. Physical therapist. Nurse."
The findings come at a time when businesses are increasingly integrating AI into software development and other functions, raising questions about the future demand for traditional technology roles.
However, the survey does not establish that AI has directly caused professionals to consider leaving the industry. Job insecurity, workplace satisfaction, compensation and changing career expectations could also influence these responses.
The Blind survey was conducted between November 6 and November 19, 2026, among 2,958 India-based professionals. Company-level figures include only employers with at least 10 responses to the relevant question.
Separately, Blind used its AI tool Clair to analyse discussions posted between January 1, 2025, and November 17, 2026, about leaving technology or software engineering for a different career.

Is Ali the first Pakistani in space?published at 03:05 GMT
- 03:05 GMT
- Not quite, although he is Pakistan's first professionally trained astronaut to travel to space.
- In October 2023, Monaco-based polar adventurer Namira Salim flew on Virgin Galactic’s Galactic 04 mission, a commercial suborbital space flight. She paid $200,000 for the ticket which she purchased in 2006.
- Suborbital flight is when a vehicle reaches outer space but flies at a speed below what is known as orbital velocity, external, which must be maintained to remain in orbit around the Earth.

Rocket launches are major spectacles in Chinapublished at 02:19 GMT
- 02:19 GMT
- Laura Bicker China correspondent
- The BBC was given rare
access to the Jiuquan Satellite launch centre in Gansu in 2024 and watched the
Shenzhou 19 launch.
- Dongfeng Space City has
been purpose built to support the launch site and China’s space programme is
celebrated on every street corner.
- The street lights are
adorned with the national flag, cartoon-like astronaut figurines and sculptures
adorn the centre of children’s parks, and plastic rockets are a centrepiece on
many traffic roundabouts.
- Hundreds of people
usually gather before a launch. They line the streets to wave flags and
brightly coloured lights as the Taikonauts (China’s name for astronauts) make
there last few steps on earth before heading to the launch site.
- It is a moment of
national pride. President Xi has declared that “to explore the vast cosmos,
develop the space industry and build China into a space power is our eternal
dream."
- We were allowed to watch
the launch from just over a kilometre away. Flames shot out of the rocket
launcher as Shenzhou 19 took to the skies and lit up the Gobi Desert with a
deafening roar.
- Image source, Getty Images
- Image caption,
- Hundreds of people gathered before the launch of Shenzhou 19 in 2024
- While in space, the Shenzhou 24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like space life sciences, aerospace medicine, and combustion.
- For example, they will look at how the space environment affects processes like vascular aging, with the hope of developing new prevention and treatment strategies.
- Ali, in particular, will study photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of space radiation and microgravity on quinoa seeds. He will return to Earth after a short stay of about a week.
- Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
Pakistani astronaut's biggest challenge? Mandarinpublished at 01:04 GMT
- 01:04 GMT
- BBC Urdu
- Image source, Reuters
- A former fighter pilot, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is no stranger to the rigorous physical and technical training sessions needed to prepare the crew for this historic mission.
- But one of the biggest challenges he faced was not quite physical - it was Mandarin.
- As all the spacecraft's switches, software, programmes and voice announcements are in Mandarin, Ali has had to familiarise himself not only with everyday, conversational Mandarin, but also technical terminology.
- Ali underwent intensive Chinese-language classes over seven months in Beijing, when he also learnt Chinese songs and Chinese poetry. He also took up calligraphy and played table tennis, Reuters news agency reported.
- "I have gone through various stages including centrifuge training, rescue and survival training and emergency procedure training, but to be honest, the biggest challenge was mastering the Chinese language," he said, according to several reports.
Mission declared a 'complete success'published at 00:47 GMT
- 00:47 GMTBreaking
- Back at Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, astronauts have just declared the Shenzhou 24 mission a "complete success".
- According to flight data and reports from the Beijing Aerospace Control Centre, Shenzhou 24 has been sent to the preset orbit, and the space craft is functioning well, a representative said in an announcement to the launch centre.
Spacecraft due to dock 3.5 hours after launchpublished at 00:43 GMT
- 00:43 GMT
- Image source, Reuters
- The Shenzhou 24 crew removed their face masks moments ago, which indicates that the pressure and air quality inside the spacecraft is relatively stable.
- Chinese authorities estimate that the spacecraft will take about three-and-a-half hours from launch to dock at the Tiangong space station.
Shenzhou 23 crew await their counterparts' arrivalpublished at 00:30 GMT
- 00:30 GMT
- The Shenzhou 24 mission is enroute into space, and the three astronauts are looking very calm, as you see on the left of this screenshot.
- On the right are the three astronauts from Shenzhou 23 mission, who entered orbit in May this year. Like us, they are tracking today's launch via livestream.
Skies turn pink as crew gets ready for launchpublished at 00:15 GMT
- 00:15 GMT
- The spacecraft will blast off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi desert in China's north-west, and in the last few minutes we've seen the skies shift from indigo and navy, to soft pinks in colour, according to a livestream from Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
- We've also seen some shots of the astronauts getting ready for the launch, repeatedly reading paper manuals - all three of them are doing that right now.
Crew received rousing send-off earlier this morningpublished at 00:08 GMT
- 00:08 GMT
- Image source, Reuters
- It's just about 10 minutes to go before the lift off and we're seeing many people gathered with their cameras and phones raised, near the spacecraft's lift-off point, trying to catch good shots of the historic moment.
- The three-men Shenzhou crew received a rousing send-off earlier this morning with hundreds of people gathered - Chinese and Pakistani flags can be seen in the crowd.
Why is this mission important for Pakistan?published at 00:06 GMT
- 00:06 GMT
- Image source, Reuters
- Image caption,
- A Long March 2F Y24 rocket carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft
- As Pakistan does not have its own spacecraft to send people to space, it is relying on China for all the important stages of this mission.
- Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.
- Ali will spend about a week on the space station, which is far shorter than the usual stay of about six months for Chinese astronauts, according to Reuters. He will return to Earth with two Chinese crew members who had arrived at the space station earlier in May.
- According to Reuters, some 50 countries have sent their citizens into space so far, but the US, China and Russia, are the only ones who have been able to do so using spacecraft developed at home.
- China's invitation to Pakistan to send astronauts to its space station is a significant development in this regard.
Why China is sending a foreigner to its space stationpublished at 23:38 GMT 24 November
- 23:38 GMT 24 November
- Laura Bicker China correspondent
- This mission is not just
a scientific achievement - it's a geopolitical statement.
- China is sending a
foreign national into space for the first time for two main reasons - science
and diplomacy.
- Forty-year-old Muhammad
Zeeshan Ali, a Pakistani Air Force Pilot is taking part in the Shenzhou-24
mission and will carry out a series of experiments in the fields of
biotechnology and photosynthetic microorganisms in a short orbital five-day
flight before returning to Earth.
- Beijing will hope this
flight will strengthen its relationship with Islamabad especially as the two
countries are marking 75 years of cooperation in space.
- China has poured billions of dollars
into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by
teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
- It is now keen to show the world
that the station has the potential to become an international research platform
rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
- All at a time when Beijing is trying
to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme and
land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.
- International partnerships help
build up influence and credibility - and so China’s message with this mission
is that it can offer other countries an opportunity to get their astronauts
into space.
China to launch Pakistani astronaut to space on historic missionpublished at 23:26 GMT 24 November
- 23:26 GMT 24 November
- Image source, Getty Images
- China's Shenzhou 24 will blast off from the Gobi desert, in the country's northwest, on its mission to carry three astronauts into space. Among them is Pakistani man Muhammad Zeeshan Ali.
- Ali will make history as the first foreign national to board China's Tiangong space station. He is joined by two Chinese astronauts, Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi.

- For Ali, it is a moment of national pride. For China, it is a step forward in its race for space dominance against the US.
- A former air force pilot, Ali is joining the mission as a payload specialist. He will stay on Tiangong for several days before returning to Earth on the Shenzhou 23, which docked at the space station earlier.

About the AIM Safety Fellowship
The AIM Safety Fellowship is a research-focused programme through which selected fellows pursue individual projects under the guidance of AIM Intelligence researchers.
Participants will explore open research questions, test their ideas, develop findings and work towards producing a manuscript suitable for submission to an appropriate academic or research venue.
Each mentor will supervise between one and three fellows, allowing participants to work closely with researchers throughout the programme. Mentorship sessions will take place weekly, providing opportunities to discuss progress, review findings and plan subsequent research activities.
The programme is intended to support practical research into AI safety and security, with an emphasis on developing meaningful research outputs.
Four Research Tracks Available
Applicants can select from four research tracks. Candidates may choose a suggested research topic or propose their own project within one of the available areas.
1. Defensive Security
This track focuses on developing approaches to protect AI systems against security vulnerabilities and potential attacks.
Suggested research topics include:
- Dynamic Tool Call Guard.
- Agentic Honeypot.
- Shadow AI Discovery.
- Defence Against Long-Horizon Attacks.
The track is supported by mentors Hanwool Albert Lee and Sungho Park.
2. Offensive Security
The offensive security track examines AI threats through adversarial research, including methods for understanding and evaluating AI agents.
Suggested research topics include:
- AI Agent Fingerprinting.
- AI Agent Profiling.
- Dynamic Benchmark for Cybersecurity Tasks.
Jongho Shin is listed as the mentor for this research area.
3. Physical AI
This track explores the safety of AI systems operating in the physical world, including applications in domestic and industrial environments.
Suggested research topics include:
- Home Safety Benchmark.
- Industrial Safety Benchmark.
- Sim-to-Real Validation.
Kihyun Kim and Chaeyun Kim are listed as mentors, with their individual mentoring arrangements still to be confirmed.
4. Frontier Safety
The frontier safety track investigates the behaviour and safety limits of advanced AI systems.
Suggested research topics include:
- Mechanistic Interpretability.
- Emerging Threats and Safety of Advanced AI.
The track is supported by Dasol Choi and Hanwool Albert Lee.
What Fellows Will Gain
The AIM Safety Fellowship is structured around supervised research and the development of academic or technical publications.
Selected fellows will benefit from:
- Research mentorship: Work directly with an AIM researcher throughout the project.
- Weekly guidance: Participate in regular meetings to discuss research progress and findings.
- Research development: Investigate a selected question and develop findings into a manuscript.
- Publication preparation: Identify an appropriate venue for submitting the completed research paper.
- Conference support: If a paper is accepted at a top-tier conference, AIM will cover registration and provide a travel grant to support attendance.
The conference support is conditional on the research paper being accepted at a top-tier conference. The announcement does not specify a guaranteed publication outcome or automatic conference funding for every fellow.

The programme is based in Seoul, South Korea. Office participation is preferred, although remote participation is also possible.

climate-energy-9cf7dcf00d.fulltext:
COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to curbing fossil fuels or scaling up climate finance.
The “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected in the final hours by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations.
Meanwhile, many developing countries criticised the lack of progress on climate finance and indecision on a proposed $120bn target for funding climate adaptation.
With stark divisions preventing agreement on the presidency-led pact, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell expressed “deep disappointment”, speaking of “scope to improve, modernise and reform” the UN climate process.
Despite a chaotic endgame that saw the overrunning COP become the longest in history, it did not end in complete failure, with many items adopted in the closing plenary.
These included fairly limited or procedural outcomes on a new “mechanism” for global “just transitions”, plus support for countries struck by climate disasters.
There was some progress beyond the negotiations, though, with growing coalitions of nations championing “roadmaps” for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels.
With the presidency promoting “electrification” as a key theme, around 80 nations also signed up to a global target of securing 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035.
Here, Carbon Brief provides in-depth analysis of all the key outcomes from Antalya, both inside and outside the COP31 negotiations.
(See Carbon Brief’s coverage of COP30, COP29, COP28, COP27, COP26, COP25, COP24, COP23, COP22, COP21 and COP20.)
Formal negotiations
Turkish and Australian leadership
Turkey and Australia presided over the longest COP in history – and failed to find consensus on their proposed “cover decision”, exposing deep fractures between countries on key issues such as fossil fuels and the need for developed nations to meet climate-finance pledges.
Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly, the talks did not “collapse” as several negotiated items were still adopted.
Rather, the rejection of the cover decision represented, for the first time, “those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer”, said one veteran observer.
Dispute over who would host COP31 – representing the “western Europe and other states” region – had gone on for three years.
In the end, the two main rivals, Turkey and Australia, agreed to a deal last year at COP30 that the summit would take place in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia acting as “president of negotiations”.
Critics questioned whether either country was well-placed to host, given their ongoing fossil-fuel expansion.
Turkey faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of the summit, while recent Carbon Brief analysis found that Australia is the third-largest CO2 exporter in history because of its fossil-fuel production.
Ahead of the summit, the presidency released four official letters outlining a vision for COP31.
The first letter, written by COP31 president Murat Kurum in April 2026, confirmed the appointment of Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as “president of the negotiations” and announced that a pre-COP would be held in Fiji in October.
The second letter, authored by both Kurum and Bowen from the Copenhagen climate ministerial in May, said that “COP31 presents a vital opportunity to further accelerate…in the areas of clean energy, electrification and resilient infrastructure”.
The third letter, published in August 2026, gave more details on the presidency’s plans for the “action agenda” – the part of the UN process that mobilises coalitions of nations and non-state actors to push climate action further.
This letter also introduced a key aim from the presidency to get countries to agree to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 (often referred to as “35 by 35”). (See: Electrification.)
The final letter, published in October ahead of the pre-COP in Fiji, said that the presidency would centre on “delivering a COP focused on accelerating implementation, electrification and resilience in an uncertain world”.
It added that “many parties have emphasised the importance of reviewing and continuously improving UNFCCC processes, to ensure it remains fit for purpose, sustainable and focused as negotiations evolve over time”, adding:
“At COP31, we will hold presidency consultations to hear parties’ views on how to strengthen UNFCCC processes, to ensure growing demands are met and to effectively deploy resources.”
The pre-COP in Fiji was held from 5-8 October and was attended by 3,000 people.
In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31.
He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”.
Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans.
COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency.
COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda.
    
        
         
                Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on…            
            
                COP31: Agenda adopted!            
        
The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found.
He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.)
Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic.
Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems.
Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns.
The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time.
On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included.
On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge.
However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision.
In the small hours of Sunday morning, half-way through the summit, Kurum announced presidency and ministerial consultations on “outstanding political issues”.
He also invited ministers to a “divan” – a group meeting, not a daybed – to discuss cross-cutting issues.
On Monday afternoon, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “presidency note” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text. (See: Cover decision.)
At a press conference, Bowen told journalists that the presidency decided to release the text “early” to allow parties to debate on it for as long as possible and acknowledged that it would need to be “refined” down.
On Wednesday evening, the presidency held its divan, where delegation heads sat in a circle and were asked to share their priorities for finding consensus in the negotiations.
Speaking at the divan, Kurum told parties that the second draft cover decision would be published that evening.
In the end, the second draft cover decision was published on Thursday.
Later that day, Kurum and Bowen spoke at a press conference, talking up their latest draft with lofty claims that it could “achieve [the] covenant of 1.5C and nothing more”.
However, the second draft was rejected by countries and civil society alike. (See: Cover decision.)
On Friday – the summit’s last scheduled day – the mood at COP soured. With few official updates, delegates relied on ever-changing rumours about when a new text might emerge.
Negotiations on other key issues also remained stuck, as civil society dubbed it the “worst COP in history” at a press conference attended by Carbon Brief.
In the evening, the presidency opened the closing plenary to gavel through non-contentious items – and announced that a new text would not be released until Saturday morning.
They were interrupted by a protester wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” and with a red noose around their neck.
As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update failed to arrive.
An open letter signed by 100 civil society organisations told the presidency it was “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had”.
As Turkish support staff started packing down the party pavilions, behind-the-scenes disputes between country ministers intensified.
Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision.
These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. (See: Cover decision.)
A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.
With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it.
Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes.
In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision.)
While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme, the global goal on adaptation, the climate finance work programme, carbon markets, long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”.
The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history.

science-mind-56bbe888f6.headline: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
science-mind-56bbe888f6.fulltext:
A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.
The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.
Advertisement
But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.
Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.
Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”
The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.
Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.
Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.
What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”
Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.
But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?
The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.
With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.
But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.
The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.
There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.
UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

ai-4b00811aa7.headline: Amazon’s Decart acquisition aims to narrow AI chip gap with Nvidia
ai-4b00811aa7.fulltext:
[Text below is TechCrunch's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.
The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.
Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.
By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.
In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.
One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.
Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.
In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”
Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”

global-economics-1115465f1a.headline: Can Amazon’s Trainium chips reduce its dependence on Nvidia? The Decart acquisition offers clues
global-economics-1115465f1a.fulltext:
Sayak BasuPublished24 Nov 2026, 11:54 PM IST Amazon said Monday that it will acquire AI startup Decart's technology and recruit its founders and other staff, thus marking the latest Big Tech deal to secure AI talent and technology. While Amazon has declined to disclose the deal's financial terms or comment on its value, Bloomberg News reported that the deal is worth around $7.5 billion. This acquisition by Amazon offers a glimpse into the company's larger ambition to reduce its dependence on Nvidia's computing ecosystem and make its own AI chips a more attractive alternative for businesses. Founded in 2023, Decart has been developing software to improve the efficiency of AI workloads across different hardware platforms, including chips from Nvidia, Amazon and Google. The company has been working with Amazon since 2025 to improve the performance of its Trainium processors. The acquisition is significant because one of the biggest obstacles to Amazon's ambition of becoming a serious AI-chip supplier has not necessarily been the hardware itself, but the software ecosystem surrounding it. The advantage that Nvidia has in artificial intelligence extends well beyond the performance of its graphics processing units (GPUs). Its CUDA software platform has become deeply embedded in the workflows of AI researchers, developers and enterprises. With its years of investment in software libraries, development tools, and optimized applications, Nvidia has become the default hardware choice for a large portion of the AI industry. Even if an alternative processor offers attractive price-performance characteristics, customers will have to consider the engineering effort required to migrate their existing workloads, adapt their software, and optimize their models for a new architecture. This is where Amazon's Trainium chips come in. They are designed to address this challenge by offering customers an alternative for training and running AI models through AWS. But Amazon needs to demonstrate that the performance and cost benefits are substantial enough to justify switching, and this is exactly where Decart will be a strategic tool for the company. Founded in 2023, the startup offers a software engine called Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), which helps companies run AI systems faster and switch more easily between a range of AI chips, including those from Nvidia, Amazon and Google. For Amazon, this technology could make Trainium more competitive without requiring the company to depend entirely on increasingly expensive investments in additional computing capacity. Amazon has spent years developing its custom silicon chips through Annapurna Labs, which it had acquired in 2015. Its portfolio includes Graviton processors for general-purpose cloud computing, Trainium for AI training and inference and Inferentia for AI inference workloads. Trainium has gained particular strategic importance following Amazon's partnership with Anthropic. Anthropic has been using AWS infrastructure to train and serve its Claude models. According to AWS, nearly one million Trainium2 chips are being used for Anthropic's workloads associated with Project Rainier. Decart itself, Karakuri, and Poolside are some of the other Trainium customers. Despite this push towards its own custom chips, Amazon is not replacing Nvidia completely, and only in August this year, AWS and Nvidia announced an expanded partnership that includes plans to deploy two million additional Nvidia GPUs across AWS infrastructure. Amazon wants to offer customers a broader choice of computing platforms while developing its own chips as a competitive alternative. This is also where Decart's technology becomes particularly interesting. Since its optimisation stack was designed to work across different chip architectures, it could help Amazon develop software capabilities that are not limited to a single hardware platform. In the AI semiconductor industry, competition is no longer limited to companies capable of manufacturing the most powerful processors. It increasingly involves software, developer tools, model compatibility, networking and the ability to extract more computing performance from existing infrastructure. For Nvidia, this integrated ecosystem has been a formidable competitive advantage. For Amazon, acquiring Decart offers an opportunity to strengthen one of the areas where competing with Nvidia has historically been difficult.
