ai-a82013b7c4.headline: As Sarvam launches a dictation API, here are the key challenges with voice AI
ai-a82013b7c4.fulltext:
Bengaluru-based AI startup Sarvam has introduced Sarvam Dictate, an API that lets developers integrate voice typing into their apps in English and 22 Indian languages.
Priced at Rs 0.50 per minute of audio, or $0.33 per hour, the service combines speech recognition with transcript editing within a single API call.
“A speech recognition model can transcribe a sentence accurately and still leave the speaker with editing to do. People restart sentences, revise what they’ve just said and use names whose spelling is hard to infer from speech alone,” the company said in a blog post.
Sarvam Dictate arrives just days after the startup launched Token Factory, an inference platform that allows enterprises, startups and businesses to access Sarvam’s proprietary models alongside global open-weight models, including Google’s Gemma and China’s DeepSeek.
The rollout sparked scrutiny over whether Sarvam had utilised government-subsidised GPU compute to host foreign-developed models. Sarvam responded to the criticism, clarifying that Token Factory operates entirely on privately procured GPUs.
How Sarvam Dictate works
Dictate pairs the startup’s Saaras v4 speech-to-text model with a version of its Sarvam 105B large language model trained for dictation. The former transcribes the audio; the latter edits the transcript.
“People do not speak the way they type. They repeat words, restart sentences, correct themselves and use names a speech model may never have hear,” Sarvam said.
According to the AI startup, Dictate factors in all of that and is designed to handle speakers switching between English and 22 Indian languages mid-sentence. It also cleans up the voice notes, removes stutters and repetitions and produces a more refined transcript.
Developers can send up to 1000 entries per request, including names and technical terms, alongside a reference document such as CRM records, a short description of the situation and a preferred writing style.
The Dictate API supports live dictation and audio recordings of up to an hour. It returns the edited text alongside the raw transcript, with a record of the vocabulary terms it applied.
Sarvam claims Dictate has already been tested on its consumer dictation app, Kivi, where users have dictated over 30 million words.
How Sarvam Dictate stacks up against global rivals
In benchmarks published alongside the launch, Sarvam AI claimed that Dictate outperforms Google’s Gemini 3.5 Transcribe and AssemblyAI Dictation across real-world dictation tests.
- English Dictations: Across 2,691 real-world English clips up to a minute long, Sarvam Dictate required only 4.2% character edits to reach the speaker’s intended text, compared to 7.0% for Gemini 3.5 Transcribe (a 40% reduction in edits) and 5.3% for AssemblyAI Dictation (a 21% reduction). On recordings longer than a minute, Dictate maintained an edge at 8.8% character edits, ahead of Gemini’s 9.9% and AssemblyAI’s 10.6%. The lower the edits required, the better the API.
- Indian Languages and Hinglish: On 1,370 dictations across 18 Indian languages, Sarvam Dictate posted an 8.8% character edit rate against Gemini 3.5 Transcribe’s 15.5%. Across Hindi, Marathi, and Urdu, the three Indic languages supported by AssemblyAI, Dictate needed 7.4% edits compared to AssemblyAI’s 15.8%. In Hinglish tests, Dictate’s edit rate dropped to 6.6%, less than half of Gemini’s 17.0% and AssemblyAI’s 14.7%.
- Domain Vocabulary and Long Conversations: On the IndicContextEval benchmark, Sarvam Dictate achieved a 15.2% word error rate (WER), outperforming Gemini 3.5 Transcribe (17.6%) and ElevenLabs Scribe v2 (18.6%), while hallucinating listed domain terms that were never spoken far less frequently. Similarly, on hour-long multilingual conversations (Indic DiarBench), Dictate recorded the lowest WER at 30.9%, beating ElevenLabs Scribe v2 (34.1%), Deepgram Nova-3 (38.3%), and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe (42.8%).
Voice AI gains momentum in India’s multilingual market
The launch of Sarvam Dictate comes at a time when startups are racing to build speech-to-text models tailored for Indian languages and Hinglish. Voice AI startups such as Gnani.ai, Bolna, and Krisp are deploying voice-first conversational AI stacks across call centers, enterprise workflows, and consumer-facing apps using proprietary speech and language models.
According to industry body NASSCOM, India’s voice AI market is projected to reach $1.8 billion by 2030, fuelled by growing demand for high-quality, real-time voice translation.
The voice AI frenzy has taken the world over. Earlier this year, Meta acquired voice AI startup Play AI for a whopping $45 million. Citing an internal memo, Bloomberg reported that Play AI’s “work in creating natural voices, along with a platform for easy voice creation, is a great match for our work and road map, across AI Characters, Meta AI, Wearables and audio content creation.”
Potential use cases of homegrown voice AI stack span sectors such as banking, financial services, and insurance (BFSI), software-as-a-service (SaaS), health, education, among others.
Real-world hurdles facing Voice AI
Despite breakthroughs in transcription accuracy, industry observers caution that deploying interactive voice AI in real-world Indian environments poses several operational challenges.
In his Reasoned newsletter, MediaNama founder and editor-in-chief Nikhil Pahwa wrote that while core speech-to-text has largely been solved for Indian accents and dialects over the past decade and a half, “voice quality is now a relatively small part of the work, and companies need to work on the job to be done, and optimising for real-world interaction, including noise and interruptions”.
Pahwa highlighted a number of friction points in live voice deployments:
- Latency and interruptions: Processing cycles involving listening, transcribing, reasoning, and speaking can introduce disconcerting delays. Moreover, Pahwa said that “interruption handling is largely unresolved with Voice AI,” noting that agents struggle when callers pause mid-thought to recall details or interrupt long-winded responses.
- Ambient Noise and Patchy Networks: Unlike sanitised product demos, real-world users, such as a shopkeeper speaking amid background chatter, create ambient audio that AI agents frequently mistake for direct commands. Patchy mobile connectivity further creates gaps in speech that models must interpret.
- Regional Grammar and Pronunciations: Pahwa warned that as voice deployments expand beyond English and Hindi into regional languages, “grammar mistakes blow up”, such as female voice personas generating male-gendered grammar, while regional variations in pronouncing identical names continue to trip up models.
- Unit Economics and Model Drift: While voice AI is often pitched at Rs 2 per minute with promises of 10x to 20x savings over human agents, Pahwa pointed out that complex, 10-minute agentic calls can cost closer to Rs 15 per minute, yielding actual savings of 3x to 5x alongside ongoing auditing costs when underlying models are updated or deprecated.

2 Indians among 11 injured in Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's financial hub
Saudi Civil Defence said one of the towers in the capital's Financial Centre had been targeted in what it described as a "terrorist attack" by the Houthi militia.
Two Indian nationals were among 11 people injured after a tower in Saudi Arabia's financial district in Riyadh was targeted in an attack carried out by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Tuesday, Saudi authorities said. The Saudi Civil Defence confirmed that the injured included two Indians, two Saudi citizens, three Nepalese nationals and four Egyptians.
In a statement posted on X, Saudi Civil Defence said one of the towers in the capital's Financial Centre had been targeted in what it described as a "terrorist attack" by the Houthi militia.
"The Civil Defence responded to an incident in which one of the towers of the Financial Centre in the city of Riyadh was subjected to a terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia, resulting in (11) injuries. They are: two citizens, two residents of Indian nationality, (3) residents of Nepalese nationality, and (4) residents of Egyptian nationality," the statement said. The authorities did not disclose the identities of the injured Indians or provide details about the severity of their injuries.
SAUDI AUTHORITIES LAUNCH INVESTIGATION
Saudi Civil Defence said emergency response teams and other relevant authorities acted immediately after the incident, implementing established procedures to protect people and property.
"The competent authorities responded to the incident immediately upon its occurrence, implemented all approved procedures and measures for dealing with such cases, and took the necessary steps to ensure the safety of lives and property," it added.
The Saudi-led coalition also confirmed the attack through its official spokesperson, describing the targeting of the Financial Centre tower as a "cowardly terrorist attack".
"The Coalition:- One of the towers of the Financial Centre was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack.- The relevant authorities are conducting an on-site investigation at the scene of the attack," the spokesperson said in a post on X. According to AFP, the witnesses identified the Public Investment Fund (PIF) skyscraper was among the buildings targeted. The PIF tower houses the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund and is the tallest skyscraper in the country.
SECOND ATTACK ON RIYADH FINANCIAL DISTRICT IN DAYS
This is the second reported attack on a tower in Riyadh's financial district in less than a week. Saudi authorities had reported another Houthi attack on Thursday, which damaged several floors of a tower in the capital's financial district, along with neighbouring buildings. The earlier strike caused material damage to the PIF tower.
According to AFP, a witness also said a vehicle fitted with a loudspeaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover. Al Jazeera reported that residents did not receive the kind of mobile phone alerts that had accompanied some previous attacks.
ATTACKS FOLLOW REPORTED STRIKES IN YEMEN
The incident comes amid escalating tensions following allegations by Yemen's Houthi-controlled authorities that Saudi-led coalition aircraft carried out airstrikes in the country's Al-Hudaydah governorate on Monday.
Yemen's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology claimed that the strikes targeted telecommunications facilities, workers' accommodation and a mosque, killing 17 workers and injuring 11 others.
In a statement posted on Telegram, the ministry said the strikes had caused extensive destruction to telecommunications infrastructure, including administrative buildings, residential facilities, a communications site and a tower. It further alleged that the damage disrupted internet and telecommunications services across several districts, leaving tens of thousands of people without basic communication facilities.

beyond-your-beat-0e00c3db26.fulltext:
Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
The Yashar party says it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party, led by Avigdor Lieberman.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has announced an agreement to unite with a right-wing opposition party in a bid to form the next Israeli government following October’s elections.
The Yashar party said on Tuesday that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
After no party managed to secure a 61-seat majority, Israel’s parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, while Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister despite the October 27 election stripping Netanyahu of his majority.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
Arab parties
The agreement between Eisenkot, whose party won 21 parliament seats, and Lieberman, whose party won seven, was unforeseen since Lieberman has been vocal about his opposition to forming a government with support from Arab parties as well as to a unity government with Netanyahu.
Lieberman had once served as foreign minister under a previous Netanyahu government but has since become a strong critic.
Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud’s alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners, including Lieberman, hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel’s Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
The path forward
Talks are also ongoing between Eisenkot, some of his “change bloc” partners and Likud on forming a unity government.
The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot after the Yashar party leader’s talks with Netanyahu’s Likud on a possible unity government.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with Arab parties.

Google denies mass layoffs in India, confirms 30 job cuts in Cloud division
Google says approximately 30 roles were eliminated in its India Cloud business following an organisational change, dismissing reports of widespread layoffs.
Google has denied reports of widespread layoffs in India, confirming that approximately 30 roles were eliminated within its Cloud division following an organisational restructuring. The clarification came on Tuesday, November 24, after reports of alleged job cuts and termination notices circulated on the employee discussion platform Blind and social media.
Responding to an X post by user Venkatesh Alla, the official Google Cloud India account described reports of mass layoffs as inaccurate and clarified the scale of the changes.
The company said: "These rumors are totally inaccurate. Last week, Google Cloud made a small organizational change in India, and approximately 30 roles were eliminated as part of a re-prioritization of work."
Google's response confirms workforce reductions within its India Cloud operations, but does not indicate a wider layoff exercise across the company's Indian workforce.
The company has not disclosed which teams were affected, where the eliminated roles were based or whether further organisational changes are planned. Google Cloud India also posted the same clarification in response to several other social media posts discussing the reports.
How the Google India layoff rumours started
The reports gained attention after an anonymous employee post on Blind raised concerns about alleged workforce reductions across Google's India-based Cloud teams.
The user described themselves as a Level 4 employee based in Bengaluru and referred to discussions circulating within Google's community on the professional forum.
The post linked to two Blind discussions and raised claims about sudden job cuts, severance arrangements and possible workforce changes in January.
Among the claims made in the post were:
- Employees across India Cloud teams were reportedly facing sudden job cuts.
- The alleged reductions were described as unrelated to individual performance.
- The post claimed employees were receiving 24-hour ultimatums to resign or face termination.
- It also mentioned severance of one month's salary and potential January workforce reductions, including voluntary exit programmes.
The anonymous poster further raised questions about whether the reported changes were limited to Cloud and developer relations teams or reflected a broader slowdown in Google's India hiring operations.
These claims remain unverified and were not confirmed by Google. The company's public response addressed the organisational change within Google Cloud India without commenting on the specific allegations concerning severance, termination notices or future workforce reductions.
Google confirms 30 roles eliminated in India Cloud
Google's clarification provides a specific figure for the workforce reduction, distinguishing the confirmed organisational change from the wider claims circulating online.
According to the company's statement, the changes involved:
- Approximately 30 roles eliminated within Google Cloud India.
- The reductions followed an organisational change made the previous week.
- Google described the exercise as a re-prioritisation of work.
- The company characterised the changes as a small organisational adjustment.
However, Google did not provide a breakdown of the affected functions or explain whether the roles were concentrated in particular locations.
The company also did not disclose whether the eliminated positions would be replaced, redistributed across other teams or absorbed into existing operations.

Trump Weighs Fresh Tariffs on India and China: What is Behind the US Trade Investigation?
The Donald Trump administration is considering raising tariffs on India, China and several other countries following an investigation into alleged unfair industrial subsidies, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could announce the findings of the investigation as early as this week, with China likely to face some of the highest tariffs, the report said.
The probe was launched in March by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) and covers 16 economies. It examines whether government subsidies and other industrial policies give foreign manufacturers an unfair advantage over American companies.
The investigation was initiated under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which empowers the USTR to investigate foreign trade practices considered unfair or discriminatory and recommend measures, including tariffs, in response.

INDIA AMONG 16 ECONOMIES UNDER INVESTIGATION
The investigation covers China, the European Union, India, Japan, South Korea and Mexico, among other economies. Taiwan, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Cambodia, Singapore, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Switzerland and Norway are also included.
Greer had earlier indicated that the investigations could lead to fresh tariffs on several major trading partners.
The USTR said the inquiries would focus on economies where there was evidence of structural excess capacity and production across manufacturing sectors. This could include persistent trade surpluses or industrial facilities operating below capacity or remaining unused.
The administration is examining whether such practices allow foreign manufacturers to produce goods at costs that undermine American industries.
INDIA ALREADY FACES ADDITIONAL US DUTIES
The latest investigation adds another layer of uncertainty to India-US trade relations. In July, the USTR had imposed an additional 10 per cent ad valorem duty on imports from India under the same provision.
Earlier this month, a senior Indian government official said the US had assured New Delhi that India would enjoy a comparative tariff advantage over competing economies under the proposed bilateral trade agreement.
“The US has assured India of a comparative tariff advantage over its competitors in the trade deal. We will have to see how the tariff framework unfolds,” the official said.
However, the official cautioned that the advantage would depend on the final tariff structure, particularly as the outcome of the second investigation initiated by the USTR against India was still awaited.
INDIA-US TRADE DEAL TALKS CONTINUE
India is seeking to conclude the first tranche of its trade agreement with the US by the end of the current financial year, the official said.
Negotiations are continuing simultaneously on the first tranche and the broader Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA).
The findings of the Section 301 investigation could influence the tariff framework being negotiated between the two countries. Any fresh duties imposed on Indian goods could also complicate New Delhi’s efforts to secure favourable market access for its exporters.
